---
title: "Display and Timing"
description: "How stimulation frequency, display refresh rate, and timing shape an FPVS experiment."
---

## Choosing a Stimulation Frequency

The base rate determines how many stimuli appear each second. FPVS studies have used a wide range of base rates, and the best choice depends on the visual process being measured, the oddball rate, the analysis strategy, and the timing limits of the display.

The examples below are organized by **base stimulation frequency**. The oddball frequency is listed when the study used a periodic oddball design.

### 3 Hz

- **Super-Recognizers, or Su-Perceivers? Insights from fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS) EEG** (Nador et al., 2025). Included a 3 Hz condition within a 3, 6, 9, and 12 Hz frequency comparison. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10548-025-01136-9){target="_blank"}
- **Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words** (Wang et al., 2025). Base rate: 3 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w){target="_blank"}
- **Preserving Harmonic Structure in FPVS-Oddball: A Two-Dimensional Cluster-Based Permutation Approach** (Hermann et al., 2026). Base rate: 3 Hz; oddball rate: 0.5 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.70361){target="_blank"}

### 4 Hz

- **Frequency-tagging EEG reveals spontaneous categorical discrimination of visual self-identity** (Galigani et al., 2025). Base rate: 4 Hz; oddball rate: 0.8 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2025.113562){target="_blank"}
- **Implicit, automatic semantic word categorisation in the left occipito-temporal cortex as revealed by fast periodic visual stimulation** (Volfart et al., 2021). Base rate: 4 Hz; category rate: 1 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2021.118228){target="_blank"}
- **Neurophysiological evidence for crossmodal (face-name) person-identity representation in the human left ventral temporal cortex** (2020). Face and name stimuli were presented at 4 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000659){target="_blank"}

### 5 Hz

- **Implicit neural sensitivity for negatively valued social and non-social visual scenes in young adults exposed to childhood adversity** (Qiao et al., 2025). Base rate: 5 Hz; oddball rate: 1.25 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291725000029){target="_blank"}
- **Visual cues of threat elicit greater steady-state electroencephalographic responses than visual reminders of death** (Valentini & Gyimes, 2019). Base rate: 5 Hz; deviant rate: 1 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsycho.2018.10.004){target="_blank"}

### 6 Hz

- **Visual periodicity reveals distinct attentional signatures for face and non-face categories** (Quek & de Heering, 2024). Base rate: 6 Hz; periodic category rates: 1.2 and 1.5 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhae228){target="_blank"}
- **Fast Periodic Visual Stimulation indexes preserved semantic memory in healthy ageing** (Milton et al., 2020). Base rate: 6 Hz; oddball rate: 1.2 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-69929-5){target="_blank"}
- **Using fast periodic visual stimulation to investigate the processing of health-related images in the human brain** (Castellano et al., 2025). Base rate: 6.075 Hz; oddball rate: 1.215 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-29515-z){target="_blank"}

### 8 Hz

- **Ensemble size perception: Its neural signature and the role of global interaction over individual items** (Jia et al., 2022). Base rate: 8 Hz; oddball rate: 1 Hz. The authors describe the method as frequency-tagging EEG/SSVEP rather than FPVS. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2022.108290){target="_blank"}

### 10 Hz

- **Linguistic and attentional factors, not statistical regularities, contribute to word-selective neural responses with FPVS-oddball paradigms** (2024). Base rate: 10 Hz; word rate: 2 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cortex.2024.01.007){target="_blank"}
- **Word-selective EEG/MEG responses in the English language obtained with fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS)** (Marchive et al., 2025). Base rate: 10 Hz; word rate: 2 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1162/imag_a_00414){target="_blank"}
- **Tracking novel visual word learning via different methods with an original FPVS-EEG approach** (Barillon et al., 2025). Base rate: 10 Hz; word rate: 2 Hz. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2025.1647925){target="_blank"}

::: {.callout-note title="There is no universally optimal base rate"}
[Retter and Schiltz (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1523/ENEURO.0426-24.2025){target="_blank"} show why the answer depends on how the response is measured. The response at the fundamental frequency, *F*, often peaks near 10 Hz, whereas the total baseline-corrected amplitude summed across harmonics often peaks below approximately 4 Hz. The rate that maximizes a general visual response may also differ from the rate that best isolates an oddball or category-selective response.
:::

## Display Refresh Rate

A display can present an FPVS base rate with perfectly even frame timing only when its refresh rate divided by the desired stimulation frequency produces a whole number. For a 60 Hz display:

| Base rate | Frames per stimulus | Frame-perfect at 60 Hz? |
|---:|---:|:---:|
| 3 Hz | 20 | Yes |
| 4 Hz | 15 | Yes |
| 5 Hz | 12 | Yes |
| 6 Hz | 10 | Yes |
| 8 Hz | 7.5 | No |
| 10 Hz | 6 | Yes |
| 12 Hz | 5 | Yes |

An 8 Hz sequence, for example, cannot use a constant number of frames per stimulus on a 60 Hz display. Alternating between frame counts would introduce timing variability. The same 8 Hz rate is frame-perfect on a 120 Hz display because each stimulus can remain visible for exactly 15 frames.

FPVS Studio detects the device's measured refresh rate and validates the requested timing whenever an experiment is launched. This prevents an incompatible stimulation rate from silently producing uneven frame timing.
